How do you structure a 45-minute system design interview?

Clarify functional and non-functional requirements (about 5 minutes), estimate QPS and storage, define the main APIs and the data model, draw a simple end-to-end design, then deep-dive into the two or three hardest parts (the bottleneck, the consistency-critical write, failure handling), and close with trade-offs and what you would do at 10x. Check in with the interviewer between steps so they can steer you to what they care about.
Which non-functional requirements do you always ask about?

Scale (users, requests per second, data size and growth), read/write ratio, latency target (p99), availability target, consistency needs (can a read be stale, for how long), durability (can we lose any data), security and compliance (PII, PHI, PCI), and geography (one region or many). Each answer removes options: "no stale reads for bookings" rules out reading from async replicas for that path.
How do you estimate QPS from daily active users?

QPS ≈ DAU × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400, then multiply by 2-5 for peak. For example 10 million DAU × 20 requests = 200 million/day ≈ 2,300/s average, ~7,000/s peak. Split reads and writes, because they scale differently. Then convert to servers: if one instance handles ~500 requests/s at your latency target (measure it), you need ~14 at peak, plus headroom for a zone failure.
What does "stateless service" mean, and how do you make a Spring Boot app stateless?

No request depends on data stored in a particular instance's memory or disk. Use JWTs or Spring Session backed by Redis instead of in-memory HttpSession, store files in object storage instead of the local disk, keep caches as disposable copies, and run scheduled jobs with a lock (ShedLock) or on one leader. Then any instance can serve any request, and the platform can add, remove or restart instances freely.
Why are sticky sessions a problem?

The LB sends a user always to the same instance because the session is in that instance's memory. Load becomes uneven, scaling in or deploying drops sessions, and a crashed node logs its users out. They are a sign of hidden state; move the session out (Redis, JWT) and turn stickiness off. Stickiness is sometimes acceptable as a cache-locality optimization when losing it is harmless.
Your traffic will be 10x next month. What do you do?

First measure: find the current bottleneck with load tests and metrics (CPU, DB connections, slow queries, p99). Then in order of cost: fix queries and indexes, add caching for hot reads, scale stateless tiers horizontally with autoscaling, add read replicas, move slow work to queues, put static content on a CDN, and raise DB connection pool and instance size. Only if writes or data size outgrow one primary, plan sharding. Re-run the load test at 10x, and check dependencies and third-party limits too.
What does a CDN cache, and how do you invalidate it?

Static assets and public, cacheable responses, according to Cache-Control and Vary headers. The cleanest invalidation is never needing it: content-hashed file names with a long max-age, and a short-lived index.html that references them. Purge APIs exist but take time to propagate. Personalized or sensitive responses should be private or no-store so a shared edge never stores them.
What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?

A popular key expires and many concurrent requests miss at once, all hitting the database and possibly taking it down. Prevent it with single-flight loading (a per-key lock or @Cacheable(sync = true) locally, a short Redis lock across nodes), serving the stale value while one request refreshes, refreshing early before expiry, and adding random jitter to TTLs so many keys do not expire together after a bulk load.
Your cache hit rate is only 40%. How do you investigate?

Check whether the key space is too large or too random (keys that include timestamps or full query strings), whether the TTL is shorter than the re-access interval, whether memory is too small so useful keys are evicted (watch the evicted keys counter), whether writes invalidate too broadly, and whether the traffic is genuinely long-tail. Fixes: normalize keys, cache at a coarser level, raise memory, switch to LFU for a stable hot set, or accept that this data is not a good cache candidate.
What is consistent hashing, and why use virtual nodes?

Nodes and keys are hashed onto the same ring; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node only moves keys on the arc next to it, about 1/N of the total, unlike hash mod N where changing N moves most keys. With only a few points per node, arcs are uneven and one node can get a big share; virtual nodes give each server many points, which evens out load and spreads a failed node's keys across all others instead of one neighbour.
How do you choose a shard key?

Pick a key with high cardinality and even distribution that appears in almost every query and keeps a transaction on one shard. For a multi-tenant EHR, tenant_id or clinic_id usually works: each clinic's data and transactions stay together. Avoid monotonically increasing keys like timestamps (all writes go to the newest shard) and keys with a few huge values (one large tenant becomes a hot shard; give it a dedicated shard).
After sharding, how do you run queries that span shards?

Avoid them on hot paths by choosing the shard key well. When needed: scatter-gather (query every shard in parallel and merge, which is as slow as the slowest shard), keep a denormalized secondary index or lookup table keyed by the other attribute (for example email → user_id), or feed a separate analytics store or search index via CDC for reporting. Global uniqueness also needs a lookup table or a globally unique ID scheme.
How do you reshard without downtime?

Use many logical shards mapped to fewer physical servers from the start, so resharding means moving whole logical shards. To move one: copy a snapshot to the new server, stream ongoing changes (binlog/CDC) until it catches up, briefly block or dual-write that shard, switch the routing map, verify, then delete the old copy. Tools like Vitess automate this for MySQL.
What does R + W > N mean?

In a leaderless replicated store with N copies, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, the read set and the write set must share at least one replica, so the read sees the latest acknowledged write (using timestamps or versions to pick it). N=3, W=2, R=2 is the common choice. W=1, R=1 is fast but can return stale data. Edge cases like sloppy quorums and concurrent writes mean it is not a full linearizability guarantee.
Is a single MySQL server CP or AP?

CAP is about replicated data under a network partition, so a single node does not really fit: if it is unreachable, it is simply unavailable, and when reachable it is consistent. The question becomes meaningful once you add replicas: reads from async replicas are available but possibly stale, and failing over to a replica that missed recent writes can lose them. Saying this shows you understand what CAP actually covers.
How does Snowflake generate IDs, and what if the clock goes backwards?

Each node builds a 64-bit ID from 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits of worker ID and a 12-bit per-millisecond sequence, so nodes never coordinate per ID and IDs sort roughly by time. If NTP moves the clock backwards, a naive generator could repeat IDs. Options: refuse to generate (throw) until the clock catches up, wait if the jump is small, or keep using the last timestamp. Worker IDs must be unique, for example from a Kubernetes StatefulSet ordinal or a lease in a coordination store.
How does an inverted index work, and why not use LIKE?

The index maps each analyzed term to a sorted posting list of document IDs (and positions). A query looks up the lists for its terms and intersects or merges them, then ranks with a relevance score like BM25. LIKE '%term%' cannot use a B+Tree index because of the leading wildcard, so it scans every row, and it has no stemming, typo tolerance or ranking. MySQL's FULLTEXT index is an inverted index too, good enough for simple cases.
How do you keep Elasticsearch in sync with MySQL?

Make MySQL the source of truth. Capture changes with an outbox table or CDC (Debezium reading the binlog), publish them to Kafka, and have an indexer consume and upsert documents using the row's version so out-of-order events do not overwrite newer data. Avoid dual writes from the request path (the two can diverge on partial failure). Keep a full reindex job for recovery, and build new indexes behind an alias so you can switch atomically.
What availability do you get from a chain of services?

Multiply the availabilities of everything a request needs. Five dependencies at 99.9% each give about 0.9995 ≈ 99.5%, which is ~44 hours of downtime a year instead of ~9. That is why long synchronous chains are dangerous. Improve it with redundancy (parallel copies multiply the failure probabilities instead), async calls for non-critical steps, timeouts with fallbacks, and caching.
How do you find single points of failure in a design?

Walk each box and arrow and ask what happens if it fails, slows down, or returns garbage. Look for the one database primary, one cache node, one LB, one region or zone, scheduled jobs on one host, DNS, secret and certificate expiry, and shared third-party APIs. For each, decide: redundancy with automatic failover, graceful degradation, or accepted risk with a recovery runbook. Then test it with failover drills.
What is a Bloom filter, and where would you use one in a design?

A compact bit array with k hash functions that answers "definitely not present" or "probably present". It has no false negatives but some false positives, and you cannot delete from a basic one. Uses: skip a database lookup for keys that do not exist (cache penetration), check whether a username or short code is probably taken, and avoid reading disk files that cannot contain a key (LSM-tree stores such as Cassandra do this).
Where do you store large files, such as scanned patient documents?

In object storage (S3, GCS) with server-side encryption, not in database BLOBs or on an app server's disk. The database stores metadata and the object key. Clients upload and download directly with short-lived pre-signed URLs after the API checks permissions, so large bytes never pass through your service. Log each access in the audit trail, and use lifecycle rules for retention.
URL shortener: 301 or 302 redirect?

301 (permanent) lets browsers and proxies cache the redirect, which cuts load but means you stop seeing repeat clicks and cannot easily change the target. 302 (or 307) is not cached by default, so every click reaches you for analytics and you can disable abusive links. Most shorteners that sell analytics use 302. You can still cache the code lookup in Redis and at the CDN with a short TTL.
URL shortener: how do you generate short codes without collisions?

Use a unique number and base62-encode it. Nodes reserve ranges of IDs (for example 10,000 at a time) from a central counter with one atomic update, so there are no collisions and no per-code coordination; a crashed node only wastes the rest of its range. Hashing the URL needs collision checks and retries. To make codes non-sequential, apply a reversible scramble to the number before encoding.
Rate limiter: why must the check be atomic, and how do you do it in Redis?

With read-then-write, two gateways can both read "1 token left" and both allow, so the limit leaks under concurrency. Run the whole read-refill-decide-write sequence as a Lua script (Redis runs a script atomically), or use atomic commands like INCR plus EXPIRE for a fixed window. In Redis Cluster all keys used by one script must hash to the same slot; use one key per client, or hash tags like {client42}.
Rate limiter: Redis is down. Fail open or fail closed?

It depends on what the limit protects. For general API quotas, fail open (allow) with a local in-memory limit per node as a rough guard, because blocking all traffic is worse than briefly exceeding quotas. For abuse-sensitive endpoints such as login, OTP or password reset, fail closed or fall back to a strict local limit. Either way, put a short timeout on the Redis call and a circuit breaker around it, and alert.
Notification system: how do you avoid sending the same message twice?

Make the request idempotent with a caller-supplied dedupKey under a unique constraint, so producer retries create nothing new. In workers, which see messages at least once, store a delivery record and check it before calling the provider, and pass the provider's idempotency token if it has one. A tiny window remains (the provider accepted but the worker crashed before recording), so true exactly-once to a device is not possible; keep that window small and the messages harmless to repeat.
Chat: how does a message reach a user connected to a different server?

Each gateway registers user → gateway node in a session registry (Redis with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats). The chat service stores the message, looks up each recipient's node and publishes to that node's channel (Redis pub/sub, or a Kafka topic per gateway group); the node pushes it down the WebSocket. If there is no entry, the user is offline: send a push notification and let the client sync on reconnect.
Chat: how do you keep messages in order and sync offline devices?

Assign a per-conversation, monotonically increasing sequence number when the message is stored; clients display by seq, never by device clock. Each device stores the last seq it saw per conversation; on reconnect it asks for seq > lastSeen and fills the gap. Gaps in received seq also tell the client it missed a message. Client retries carry a clientMsgId so a resend does not create a duplicate.
Booking: how do you prevent two patients booking the same slot?

Let the database decide with one atomic conditional update: UPDATE slot SET status = 'BOOKED' … WHERE id = ? AND status = 'OPEN', and treat 0 rows updated as 409 Conflict. InnoDB locks the row, so the second transaction waits, then sees the committed status and matches nothing. Back it up with a unique index (for example on a generated "active slot" column), and make the POST idempotent so a client retry does not book twice or show a false conflict. Do not use check-then-insert without a lock.
Booking: how do you hold a slot while the patient fills in the form?

Set the slot to HELD with held_by and held_until = now + 5 minutes using the same conditional-update pattern. Confirming requires held_by to match or the hold to have expired. Because the booking condition treats expired holds as open, correctness does not depend on a cleanup job. Limit holds per patient to stop someone holding a whole day of slots.
Booking: how do you design the audit trail for patient data?

Record every view and change of patient data: timestamp, actor and role, action, patient ID, entity and ID, source IP or device, and a request correlation ID. Write changes to the audit table in the same transaction as the data so they cannot diverge; log reads asynchronously but reliably (outbox or queue). Make it append-only (no update or delete permissions), copy it to write-once storage, restrict who can read it, and keep it for the retention period your compliance team sets. Avoid copying clinical content into the log itself.
A queue between two services keeps growing. What do you do?

Find out whether producers spiked or consumers slowed (a failing dependency, poison messages retried forever, a slow query). Short term: scale consumers up to the partition count, shed or defer low-priority work, move poison messages to a DLQ. Longer term: autoscale on lag, add partitions if consumer parallelism is the limit, batch writes, and set a retention or TTL policy so an unbounded backlog cannot fill the broker. See Kafka for consumer lag specifics.
How do you handle a "celebrity" hot key?

One key (a famous user's profile, a viral link) gets so much traffic that its single shard or cache node saturates. Cache it in process on every app node for a few seconds, replicate it under several suffixed keys and read a random one, or put a CDN in front if it is public. For writes (likes, counters), aggregate in memory or in sharded counters and flush periodically instead of updating one row per event.
SQL vs NoSQL: which store do you pick for a given workload?

| Relational (MySQL, PostgreSQL) | Document (MongoDB) | Wide-column (Cassandra) | Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB)
Data shape | Related entities, fixed schema | Nested aggregates, flexible fields | Partitioned rows, sorted by a clustering key | Opaque value per key
Transactions | Full ACID across tables | Multi-document transactions, best kept small | Per partition; lightweight transactions are costly | Per key (DynamoDB has limited transactions)
Queries | Ad hoc joins and aggregates | Rich queries within a collection | Only by partition key (design tables per query) | Get and put by key
Write scaling | One primary, then sharding | Built-in sharding | Linear, masterless | Very high, partitioned
Good fit | Appointments, billing, orders | Product catalogues, form-like clinical documents | Chat history, time series, event logs | Sessions, caches, URL lookups, rate limits
Rule of thumb: start with a relational database when you need transactions and the queries are not fully known yet; choose NoSQL for a specific access pattern at a scale or shape that SQL handles badly, and say which pattern drives the choice. Many designs use both.
Cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind: which and when?

| Cache-aside | Write-through | Write-behind (write-back)
Who fills the cache | The app, on a miss | Every write goes through the cache to the DB | Writes land in the cache; flushed to DB later
Write latency | DB write + cache delete | Higher: cache and DB synchronously | Lowest
Staleness | Up to TTL, or a short race window | Low | Low in cache, DB lags behind
Data loss risk | None (DB is the truth) | None | Unflushed writes lost if the cache fails
Cache contents | Only what is read | Everything written, even never-read data | Everything written
Best for | General read-heavy data | Data read right after writing | High-rate counters, metrics, non-critical aggregates
Rule of thumb: default to cache-aside with a TTL. Use write-through when readers must see fresh values immediately, and write-behind only for data you can afford to lose or rebuild, never for clinical or financial records.
Sharding vs replication vs partitioning: what does each solve?

| Replication | Partitioning (one server) | Sharding
What it does | Full copies of the same data on several nodes | Splits a table into pieces on the same server | Splits rows across servers by a shard key
Solves | Read scaling, high availability, backups | Partition pruning, cheap drop of old data | Write throughput and data size beyond one node
Does not solve | Write throughput, data size | Capacity of one server | Availability by itself (each shard still needs replicas)
New problems | Replica lag, failover | Partition key must be in the primary key and queries | Cross-shard joins, transactions, resharding
MySQL example | Primary + read replicas, Group Replication | PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) | Vitess, or app-level routing by tenant_id
Rule of thumb: replicate for availability and reads, partition for maintenance of big tables, and shard only when one primary can no longer take the writes or the data. Real systems combine them: every shard is replicated.
Strong vs eventual consistency: how do you decide per feature?

| Strong (linearizable) | Eventual
Read guarantee | Always the latest committed write | May be stale; converges if writes stop
Latency | Higher: wait for the leader or a quorum | Lower: any nearby replica answers
During a partition | Some requests fail or wait | Keeps answering
Conflict handling | Prevented up front | Needs last-writer-wins, versions or merge logic
Use for | Slot booking, payments, inventory, medication orders | Feeds, view counts, search results, analytics, notifications list
Rule of thumb: ask what a stale or conflicting read costs. If it causes a wrong action (double booking, overselling, a wrong dose), make that path strongly consistent; everything else can be eventual, usually with read-your-writes for the user who made the change.
Polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket: how do you push updates to clients?

| Short polling | Long polling | Server-Sent Events | WebSocket
Direction | Client pulls | Client pulls, server holds the request | Server to client only | Both ways
Latency | Up to the poll interval | Near real time | Real time | Real time
Cost | Many empty requests | One open request per client, re-opened per message | One long HTTP response; auto-reconnect built in | One persistent connection; stateful servers
Infrastructure | Plain HTTP, cache friendly | Plain HTTP; watch timeouts | Plain HTTP; proxies must not buffer | Needs upgrade support in LB and proxies
Fits | Job status every 10 s, dashboards | Legacy clients needing push | Live feeds, notifications, progress | Chat, collaboration, games
Rule of thumb: poll when a few seconds of delay is fine, use SSE when only the server pushes, and use WebSocket when both sides send frequently. Mobile apps in the background need platform push (APNs/FCM) whichever you choose.
Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices: what do you choose for a new product?

| Monolith | Modular monolith | Microservices
Team size it suits | One small team | One to a few teams | Many teams owning separate domains
Deployment | One unit | One unit, enforced module boundaries | Independent per service
Data | One shared schema | One database, tables owned per module | Database per service, eventual consistency
Operational cost | Lowest | Low | High: discovery, tracing, CI/CD per service, on-call
Changing boundaries | Easy but tends to tangle | Easy: refactor inside one codebase | Expensive: APIs and data migrations
Rule of thumb: for a new product with unclear domains, start with a modular monolith (Spring Modulith or package-level boundaries) and extract a service only when a module needs independent scaling, deployment or ownership. Details are in Microservices.
